Hi [~accountid:626c24971a4eb30069d28197], 

We have now received a response from our outside counsel. For reference, please find the memo attached. As you can see the risk of breach of contract is determined to be high as both Uber and Yango’s ToS prohibit price scraping. Furthermore, criminal liability can be imposed on Bolt and potentially Bolt employees. The risks of criminal liability have been determined to be low but can never be removed. *There is no risk-free way to conduct route fare+ETA window shopping in the RH industry and legal can never green-light such activities.* 

The below process should be followed in Finland in relation to Uber and Yango. 

When ToS  prohibit data extraction by account holder (which is the case), ability to keep legal risks in check rests on 2 key factors: 

(i) security process and protocol to ensure that activity cannot be easily identified by the target, and

(ii) distancing Bolt from the data collection activity itself and having a legal recourse to a 3rd party service provider.

Basic rule in all cases where target’s ToS prohibits data extraction (which is the case with Uber and Yango) has to be: 

# Engage 3rd party under a dataset acquisition agreement (as opposed to instruction and service agreement) with full indemnifications for Bolt’s benefit under acceptable risk-premium. This is the preferred route but it requires that the 3rd party provider is willing to provide us with full indemnification which could be hard to find. Research on this should be done by the local team to see what the options are [~accountid:626c24971a4eb30069d28197]. 
# If we can’t engage a 3rd party we should do it in-house instead with a focus on security arrangements. The focus should at all times be to keep it small-scale and low-frequency as it is unlikely to cause considerable harm or damage and therefore, such activities would be less vulnerable.

Furthermore, we need to determine which method will be used by the 3rd party provider as we need to confirm that the method ensures both (i) limited scale of the activity; and (ii) better security protocol.  

I would also like to highlight that Bolt’s liability would be unlimited in a case of breach of contract. 

I suggest you read through this advice and revert with your proposed actions on the window shopping. If we want to use a 3rd party provider we need to initiate discussions with specific vendors in order to determine if they fulfil our requirements on security protocols and indemnification. 

Best regards, 

Michelle

h3. *Feedback from the BSS team:*

*Julio:*

In the African region, we come across these types of fraud cases:

* [starting and ending the trip|https://nigeria-admin.bolt.eu/order/Orders/order/1270431142/1429579847] without the rider (the driver did not pick up the rider). The business client sends us an overview of the rides that they don’t recognize and then we can action them accordingly. Another [example|https://nigeria-admin.bolt.eu/order/Orders/order/1266719094/1424346388]. [Client BH ticket|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/188948439]
* [OTP fraud|https://ghana-admin.bolt.eu/order/Orders/order/1312756772/1446285699/] - where drivers request the OTP from unknowing riders who then share this sensitive information with the driver. Riders are unaware and the driver is telling them they need this intel in order to start the ride.

In the future, we are going to conduct CCPOs’ deep dives in order to find patterns and come up with effective solutions.

*Lais:*

In the UK, we haven’t started conducting deep dives yet, but one type of fraud we have noticed is related to Business Campaigns.

* The business campaigns are currently focused on new users and provide a certain discount for the first X rides in a specific timeframe. We have had examples in which companies start creating new accounts in order to be included in the new round of campaigns. So whenever we pick up a ticket on the subject, it’s important to keep an eye on possible duplicate accounts. Example here: [link 1 |https://admin.bolt.eu/business/BusinessCompany/company/235992]/ [link 2|https://admin.bolt.eu/business/BusinessCompany/company/237646] / [link 3|https://admin.bolt.eu/business/BusinessCompany/company/224092] / [ticket|https://bolt.zendesk.com/agent/tickets/35837750]

*Justina:*

In Lithuania, we often get tickets from the business administrators flagging cases as a fraud when it's actually not fraud (at least not from our side). Case example: business account administrator sends us proof of payment for the trip which is not presented on their business portal. In most cases, it happens because companies let their employees add the company's business card directly to the employee's personal app and they choose that card instead of the business payment method identified with the company’s name.

*Andrei:*

In the RO market, we encounter mainly two types of fraudulent behavior from drivers. [The first|https://europe-admin.bolt.eu/order/Orders/order/1214395869/1359595727] example is where they accept the trip and then contact the user in order to get more info about the trip details (destination/ price). If they consider those details unsatisfactory, the ride will not be canceled and the driver will stay in one place or move around in the city waiting for the rider to cancel eventually. [The second|https://europe-admin.bolt.eu/order/Orders/order/1130843494/1255605954] ([x2|https://europe-admin.bolt.eu/order/Orders/order/1130950580/1255742565]) type of case is when the driver and the rider are acquainted and will plan a trip with the company card (if the policy allows it), driving for hours around the city.

*Guilherme:*

In the PT market, I could notice mainly these two fraud scenarios cases recently. *For example:*

* The driver did not finish the ride after arriving at the destination point. [Order|https://westeurope-admin.bolt.eu/order/Orders/order/974915575/1156347870] / [Order|https://westeurope-admin.bolt.eu/order/Orders/order/974915575/1156347870].

Scenario: business admin reports the rides were overcharged after ending the trip. Usually, drivers finish the ride later to overcharge the client.

* The driver started and ended the trip without the rider. [Order|https://westeurope-admin.bolt.eu/order/Orders/order/991236949/1189544392].

Hey team,

* *The underlying issue here being that Bolt acts as an intermediary/ platform operator, and hence not taking any liability for driver caused damage?* 

_This shouldn’t come as a surprise for anyone internally. It has been repeated over and over in every occasion, in every training. And the T&C’s - these just foster this stance._

However *in all our markets the are some Business customers who push back on this. In most cases we have been able to explain:*

* how we monitor driver compliance, 
* how drivers have mandatory 3rd party liability insurance in place with wide coverage, 
* maybe we can also acquire some stats on how few loss events actually take place during Business rides, 
* etc, 

*and close these deals nevertheless because overall our value prop is higher* (convenience, pricing, etc) than the company's who can offer this liability absorption but not really anything else.

*And yes, we have and will loose some customers to this. So far this has been deemed acceptable by Business leadership* as we have plenty of fish in the sea.

*And it’s up to the Business leadership to initiate discussions should that not be the case anymore,* by first:

* aligning with Rides, Public Policy and Legal teams what would it mean if we started taking up liability for drivers (for Business rides) in the particular market (reclassification risk to start with), and equally;
* aligning with Finance and Insurance teams what would it mean for our financial exposure, and how to mitigate these risks.

Once alignment is reached and respective solutions implemented then adjusting the T&C’s is a mere formality. [~accountid:631754a0ea661fd37d501b4e] [~accountid:60d6dd5cc90cb20068954dfc] 

Until then (speaking from practice from other markets):

* these requests by customers are first raised to Legal in several cases,
* we have the discussions we’re having now, 
* and then over time it’s raised less and less as the Business team already knows the drill. 

Ofc every now and then it still reaches Legal as customers raise it from another angle, sales badgers miss it, or whatnot, but it is what it is until there are no such customers left, or we break the cycle as described above. 



*As an alternative* we could explore what commitments could we make towards customers *in relation to facilitating claims from users/customers to drivers' insurers* should a loss event occur.

[~accountid:631754a0ea661fd37d501b4e] [~accountid:60d6dd5cc90cb20068954dfc] should that strike as a viable option I suggest to reach out to Insurance and CS teams first to see what added value we could offer here to make our customers feel comfortable that they nor their users are left alone hunting down liable drivers.

But realistically - just adding a clause to the T&C’s about customer’s option to reach out to our customer support is not gonna make the above go away. _In each case Legal does not object adding such soft statements to the T&C’s if the team truly thinks this is the blocker here._

Do let me know what you think, and let’s go from there.

A.

-The main challenge are requirements 5 and 6. Others are already addressed by the changes described under “Option 1” in this document:- [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/4292707249/2023+Feb+-+Entrance+detection+model+integration+options#Option-1---Eater-side|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/4292707249/2023+Feb+-+Entrance+detection+model+integration+options#Option-1---Eater-side|smart-link] 

-The challenge stems from the fact that once the overridden coordinates are used to place an order they will get stored into the delivery_order_history table, which then becomes a provider for location-suggestions-delivery. Since they cannot be altered, we need to store the original-overridden coordinates mapping somewhere. We face a similar problem with the “Delivery Location” case, although here we shouldn’t have a requirement to always hold and retrieve the exact same location that the user previously confirmed (we should confirm this with Eater teams though). An overridden location will get stored as a “delivery location” as soon as the user selects a location suggestion from the list or the “current location” option.-

-We will address the two cases separately.-

-For the Delivery Location case:-

* -We will design the system so that the Delivery User table ALWAYS holds original coordinates. To override them we will modify the flow as described in the “Flow 1” subsection:- [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/4292707249/2023+Feb+-+Entrance+detection+model+integration+options#Flow-1---Ordering-to-the-previous-delivery-location|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/4292707249/2023+Feb+-+Entrance+detection+model+integration+options#Flow-1---Ordering-to-the-previous-delivery-location|smart-link] 
* -The system needs to ensure that overridden coords will never get stored in the delivery_user table. To do that we will do the following:-
** -At serving time, suggest overridden coordinates, but enhance the Suggestion interface with a new field called original_coordinates  holding the original lat/lng values.-
** -When the user selects a suggestion we will receive a /recordDeliveryLocationEntered call. The request body contains all requested suggestions as they were received from backend. We can identify which suggestion was selected by comparing lat and lng fields with the lat and lng fields of the request. We can then call setDeliveryLocation using the original_lat/orginal_lng coordinates instead of the suggestion lat and lng (the overridden ones)-
** -This won't work as smoothly for Google suggestions, because they lack lat and lng at serving time. Due to to a long-lasting bug, eater apps never send selected_suggestion_index as they should and instead always send selected_current_location which contains both the coordinates and the address. So instead of the default strategy, we can identify the clicked suggestion by looking at selected_current_location.address and comparing it with the suggestion addresses. To retrieve the original coordinates, we can issue a  getPlaceDetails call, and compare the result with the lat/lng received.-
** -This wont’t work as smoothly for the “current location” case either. Here we can issue a reverse geocoding call using gps_lat and gps_lng and compare the result with what we receive in the request body.-

-For the Delivery History case:-

-A robust solution would involve decoupling LSD from this source of data and using a Geo-owned provider, populated in a similar manner as the current provider, but which we can alter and amend according to our needs. A long term solution will look something like this:-

* -propagate place_ids through the delivery system. This means eater apps and delivery backend should know about place_ids: this means API changes, database changes, app code changes, SNS/SQS interface changes etc.-
* -when location-suggestions-delivery (LSD) sends overridden coordinates, it could re-encode the associated place_id to contain the original coordinates as well-
* -a new location-suggestions-delivery-orders (LSDO) service would be created, which will become the new “delivery history” provider for LSD. It would subscribe to the delivery-order SNS and would store the delivery order data into its own storage system (could be Elasticsearch or SQL).-
* -When LSDO receives a new order from the queue, it would decode the place_id and store both sets of coordinates in its system-
* -when LSD serves suggestions having LSDO as a provider, it would decode the place-id and decide whether to use original or overridden coords-

-Naturally, this has a very high cost in terms of development time so we have to come up with some quicker albeit temporary solution.-

Here’s a potential alternative plan:

* spin up a new database which will hold a translation table between overridden coordinates and original coordinates. LSD will own it. We will add an InMemoryStore for good measure.
* when we receive a {{recordDeliveryLocationEntered}} event or a request from the {{getDeliveryLocation}} flow to override previous eater location with model location: store an entry in the translation table
* create a new post-processor in LSD which will translate these coordinates into original coordinates (IF we are on the control branch of an experiment!)

PINT team responded and we cannot use existing audit-log service for our needs.

Here are couple of options we have:

# We build a dedicated change log / data history service for ourselves only. It would be a generic service which can hold data about any entity we have. This means duplicating all the data into separate isolated unit which is independent from current DB. Possibly brand new database, example: _taxify_business_changelog/history._
## *Pros*
### Isolated and independent service to deal with history
### Separately scalable and accessible
## *Cons*
### No transactional support if it is separate database and only access over network calls
### Not easy to join history to back main entities in one go, have to call separate service all the time
# We can also do 1) but within the same database context
## *Pros*
### Transaction support for DB queries
### Can easily join historic info with main entity queries
## *Cons*
### As we’ll keep copying lots of data over into change log tables, over time dataset grows large and we cannot separately scale usage of this data.
# We update existing tables to be ledger tables. Instead of updating data in place, we’ll always insert a new row instead.
## *Pros*
### System is by design keeping track of the history.
#### Example: global user linking table is a ledger table.
## *Cons*
### We have lot’s of primary key dependencies in other tables, which means we would need to update references entities in all the tables when main entity gets a new entry.
### Or update existing entity tables have a separate field for secondary ID field, which stays the same.
#### This however makes it really difficult to understand the schema, because people are used to using primary keys (ids) to reference things
# We split mutable revision data and stable data of the entities. This means we have stable data like primary key IDs, created/last_update fields etc. on the main entity table but data itself is in a separate ledger table.
## *Example*
### {code:sql}// business_user_group
id, created, last_update, business_user_group_revision_id
1, ...., ..., 2

// business_user_group_revision
id, created, last_update, business_user_group_id, name, policy_id, revision_metadata_id
...
2, ...., ..., 1, "My Best Group", 1, 2

// revision_metadata
id, created, last_update, entity_type, entity_id
1, ..., ..., bolt-operations, 100
2, ..., ..., business-admin, 200{code}
## *Pros*
### Main entities we use today stay intact, we can always reference them through primary key ID
### We keep track of all the changes in separate revision table by default, it’s built into system architecture
## *Cons*
### We have to always join minimally 2 tables, given some of the entities are already used in complex queries, this will increase queries complexity.
# History tables for each of entities we have, which are 1:1 copies of the main tables. We keep  updating current entities in place as today but copy over previous values before the update to history table.
## *Pros*
### Relatively easy to implement
## *Cons*
### Lots of data duplication, system architecture actually gets more complex because we have side track of data for history instead of building system to keep history by design, like in points 3,4 🔝  would do.

Hi there!

To give a bit of context: The fraud team deals with bigger cases of financial fraud or user patterns with a significant business case. The fraud team does not look at users on an individual level unless it is a clear false positive case. And even in those cases, it is rather for us to finetune our rules and restrictions for a more positive user experience for *good* users.

Further, what you have here is a *refund/promo fraud* (social engineering) case which, in general, is overall dependent on CS processes and procedures. Think of it this way - the user is just requesting a refund/promo and we are giving them the satisfactions, therefore we are allowing them to financially gain.

Hence, I can suggest you follow your local processes in regard to users making bad reports/requesting refunds or compensations; and possibly raise this with your leads if you find issues with the processes. It is up to you how to action the user.

On a different note, kindly be more precise in your escalations in the future and give as many details as possible about your case. Some examples to consider or think about: _What makes this case significant? How did you discover the matter? What is the current situation? What is suspicious in your opinion exactly? What have you already done? Who have you consulted on the matter?_ *_What is the expected outcome? What would you like us or propose to do? What is the impact of this issue on GMV and count? What is the urgency of the issue?_*

# Different parts of the UK will have the submission process set up differently.  

* In person submission - driver visits the hub, we take pictures of their documents with our tables or we use their device to upload/re-upload docs on the driver portal
* Online submission - drivers is sent a link to resubmit/submit their documents via the driver portal/registration page
* Email submission - at times drivers will email us documents via Infobip if they are struggling to use the driver portal

From a business perspective it is our intention to make this process as smooth as possible, especially as our driver demographic is quite often older and less tech-savvy. As of at least autumn of last year, after Ops asks Regs to look into licensing a new area, Regs will request that Ops obtain an office in the licensing area 

To guide that search, Regs asks for:

*  a map with a compass and scale 
* confirmation that the location has existing B1 (or E) use class 
* confirmation that the landlord has been informed that Bolt intends to apply for COLU for the office 

Once these requirements are met, Ops brings the proposed office to Legal for your review. 

Bolt never asks for consent from the landlord for us to apply for sui generis planning permission because we always apply for E(g)i.  *However, when our COLU application is being reviewed, the respective Planning Department may respond and elect to automatically grant us sui generis. I believe this is where the breakdown in the process occurs.* 

I have audited our offices and can confirm that the below have been granted sui generis use class without the landlord’s initial consent or subsequent knowledge. These offices are: 

* Blackburn and Darwen
* Possibly Brighton & Hove 
* Sefton

I’d note that our planning permission records are _very_ spotty, it's likely that there are 1-2 more of these cases. I will speak with MSG to see where we can fill the gaps.

Hi there Balint!

In order to understand this case, let’s start with our fraud logic. 🙂 

The main idea of fraud checks is to assess the user and their risk. If there are some irregularities detected either through actions or relations, an additional score or decision is applied to the user based on this. Business users in this sense are not treated differently, but they do have the additional factor of the business itself in play. Meaning that businesses with for example payment problems will add additional risk for the user itself and this prompts the extra actions. 

The overall recovery (or a way out of restrictions) for risky users is to verify themselves such as was prompted in this case but verification is also capped. In case there are further suspicious factors in play (the risk and score are very high) then the verification will not equal the user being “freed” of restrictions. This relationship is carefully analysed and set based on different scenarios. This is exactly what happened with this user - they followed the recovery and were successfully verified, however, the risk indicators are high due to unusual behaviour. 

Now coming to the actual reason behind the high score and risk. The user and business fell into some suspicious fraud indicators. In general, a new business (without good history) with one new user immediately arranged multiple expensive journeys and this is highly irregular/suspicious. 

*What can be done for the client?* You advise the client that any restrictions should be gone on Monday as well as to avoid pre-booking or arranging many journeys at the same time, at least until Monday. I can see that they now have incurred some good payments - can be trusted.  So I can take them up as an example at the beginning of next week to review further and possibly the need to further adjust some of the thresholds. We are not able to make such changes before weekends.

It’s tough for us to bill a customer for a high-price journey if we don’t have the logs/data to show that the service was requested. The driver shouldn’t have any legitimate reason for finishing the ride at another destination than was requested through the app. Doing so goes against our app guidelines and conditions. I can see that the passenger was rejected an update on multiple occasions and was notified accordingly. I highly doubt that the rider was having a technical issue as I can see the attempts and responses. There was a legitimate reason for this rejection. The correct process would have been to end the journey they had initially reserved and place a new order for any extra stops or destinations. 

Essentially, we’ve refunded because this ride wasn’t logged/approved in the App. The ride request had a really low prediction and there’s no destination change logged/approved in the App to justify the route the driver made. If the payment were successful, a refund wouldn’t happen from our side.

*The main point is that please don’t compensate the driver this amount back in these cases.* The drivers must be educated that if the passenger requests a new destination, they must log that in the App and wait for approval. *If we don’t approve the change, they have to follow the message that is displayed to them in the App*. Check this KB article about it [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7643088163474|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/7643088163474]

# the option of training needs to be optional, this means we cant prohibit their access by forcing them to do it prior to driving. We can make it difficult to opt out of to a degree (however you see fit) but there needs to be the opt out option for both black cabs and PHV training; and

The reason this is important is because a key reclassification argument is that an employer by ordinary nature can place control over an employee/worker and require them to complete mandatory training for their role - by not having this in place it removes validity of that argument towards employee/worker- therefore tips the scales away from Worker back to IC in analysis from an employment law perspective. 

If there is resistance to do this from a global standpoint, HQ may want to consider checking what the reclassification risk of retaining this ‘as is’  is in other EU countries as well before this becomes ammunition in future disputes. *Estonian labour law* 

# *Is the market subject to laws where an employment relationship can be deemed or implied?* Yes
# *Is there any evidence that platforms are under scrutiny under the legal system (litigation etc)?* No
# *Is the relevant test subject to express presumption criteria?* In a dispute over the nature of the contract (if the contract has the characteristics of both an employment and another contract), the parties are deemed to have an employment relationship unless the employer proves otherwise.
# *Are RSAs expressly considered by a court or any law to imply an employment relationship?* The main characteristic of the employment contract is the submission to the employer’s management and control. The greater the control over a person (contractor), the more likely he/she is considered an employee. To refute the employment presumption set forth in § 1 (2) of the Employment Contracts Act, the alleged employer must prove above all that the employee was not subject to its management and control and was largely independent in choosing the way, time and place of doing the work.
# *Can claims be made in respect of past periods (i.e. for previously withheld earnings?* Yes, up to 3 years
# *Who is able to take action against Bolt? Couriers / group action / regulators?* Couriers or group action. But once the Directive is adopted, and after it is transported into the local law, it will become very likely that Labour or Tax authorities would use its ex-officio right to launch investigations into related subjects. The Directive will create a legal presumption of an employment relationship between platforms and persons performing platform work (if the 3 out 5 criteria are met).  Member States will be required to establish a framework for effective implementation of the legal presumption through appropriate measures, it will also mean strengthening controls and field inspections.
# *Is there any evidence the authorities have considered couriers eligible for employment benefits in the past (e.g. tax authorities, pension authorities etc)?* No
# *What is the level of access to justice in a market (e.g. high state duties, requirement to have a representative etc)?* Employment matters are state fee free and access to employment litigation is well established.
# *Can claims be made to reclassify all couriers of the platform in a market at once?* No. Court rulings have legal effect only for the parties of the dispute. So no court ruling on reclassification would be automatically applicable to all couriers. But the effect of a court precedent may trigger similar court actions.

left join ng_public.admin_system_city asc2  on asc2.id = upu.user_home_city_id 
where first_market_vertical_purchase is not null
and first_market_vertical_purchase between date('') and date('')
group by 1,2,3,4,5{noformat}



Market-First Delivery user (cohorted to install, 14d)

{noformat}select 'Eaters' as audience, 'common' as platfrom, install_date as day, country, city, count(distinct ffo.master_user_id) as first_market_delivery_orders_cohorted_b_{cohort_days}
from ng_public.etl_first_finished_order_for_user ffo
LEFT JOIN ng_public.etl_first_order_attribution_channel AS attr ON attr.master_user_id = ffo.master_user_id
LEFT JOIN ng_delivery.delivery_provider_provider_trait AS pt
      ON ffo.provider_id = pt.provider_id
where date_diff('day',install_date, ffo.created_date) < {cohort_days}
and  pt.trait_id = 145
group by 1,2,3,4,5{noformat}



Market-First Bolt users (cohorted to install, 14d)

{noformat}select 'Eaters' as audience, 'common' as platfrom, install_date as day, country, city, count(distinct ffo.master_user_id) as market_first_bolt_users_cohorted_b_{cohort_days}
from ng_public.etl_first_finished_order_for_user ffo
LEFT JOIN ng_public.etl_first_order_attribution_channel AS attr ON attr.master_user_id = ffo.master_user_id
LEFT JOIN ng_delivery.delivery_provider_provider_trait AS pt
      ON ffo.provider_id = pt.provider_id 
left join ng_public.etl_user_products_usage upu on ffo.master_user_id = upu.user_id
where date_diff('day',install_date, ffo.created_date) < {cohort_days}
and pt.trait_id = 145
and first_vertical = 'Market'

We can have legally binding agreement, this is regulated by applicable legislation, BUT there are some limitations:

# The cost per person should be significant or significantly higher than allocated budget per person per year.
# The agreement must be timed and the binding length shouldn’t be unreasonably long (for example - if the cost per course/session is twice the yearly budget, it could be reasonable to bind the person for a year). 
# The cost we could reclaim should be proportional - meaning, every elapsed month reduces the maximum amount we can reclaim.
# There should be exceptions for redundancy and termination based on a MA.



If the cost per person is about ~250 EUR, I’d say that this is in budget and the agreement wouldn’t be legally enforceable.

Hi! 

1.1 (a): Wilful misconduct is a defined term under Estonian laws and we do not want to add any specific examples to the agreement as it would need to be analysed and decided on case by case basis.

Definition of wilful misconduct: “the will to bring about an unlawful consequence upon the creation, performance or termination of an obligation.”

To provide you more context, other forms of culpability are negligence and gross negligence which, as regulated under the agreement, would not be excluded from indemnification being applicable.

 Negligence: “failure to exercise necessary care”

 Gross negligence: “failure to exercise necessary care to a material extent”

1.4 Under the agreement the company is the one with the obligation to indemnify the indemnitee. Thus, it must also be the company who needs to assess whether the conditions (as set out in the agreement) for the indemnitee to be indemnified are met. We cannot extend such assessment making discretion to indemnitee’s legal counsel. 

Additionally, the indemnification agreement is a group-wide template approved by Bolt, and as a general rule no changes can be made to the approved version. 

I hope the above is clear and you have the necessary comfort to sign the agreement.

При цьому, варто зазначити, що у особистих розмовах я зобов’язався дотримуватись вимог, що передавали співробітники компанії (актуальність наповнення накшталт тарифів, використання колірної палітри тощо; фактично, тих, які описані у положеннях обов’язків агента) та продовжую дотримуватись таких домовленостей без будь-який додаткових договорів. Вважаю, що історія нашої взаємодії за минулі роки не дала ні натяку на негативні інсинуації, що потребували б додаткових юридичних зобов’язань._
# _Так, згідно цього договору (пункт 1.5) Bolt надає мені право використовувати доменне ім’я, а значить і вебсайт, який його має – а значить, не перешкоджає нашій діяльності. Проте, виникає логічне запитання – я і так його використовую тільки в цілях забезпечення нашої плідної співпраці, але після підписання втрачаю право власності на нього, хоча назва «boltdriver» не є торгівельною маркою і отримання такого доменного імені не вимагало від мене жодних підтверджень. Тоді навіщо ж передавати таке право власності Вам?_
# _Звичайно, я не вбачаю великих ризиків, погоджуючись на пунки розділу «4. Agent’s Obligations», проте складно підписатись під можливістю швидко та на постійні основі забезпечувати compliance-аспект, адже певні відмінності між законодавством України та країн ЄС має значні відмінності (до прикладу, різняться вимоги у сфері політик конфіденційності, обробки, зберігання та використання персональних даних тощо), які й допомогають нам виконувати наші функції у рамках нашої взаємодії (залучати водіїв, залучати автопарки, використовувати інструменти онлайн- та офлайн-реклами тощо із подальшою обробкою результатів)._
# _На момент купівлі доменного імені та створення вебсайту не було обговорено необхідність відповідності його до Bolt’s Supplier Code of Conduct (пункт 4.1.3), адже такого розділу на вебсайті Bolt не існувало. Досягення такої відповідності, потребуватиме певного періоду часу, який не можливо передбачити наразі._
# _Звичайно, англійська мова є інструментом ведення міжнародного бізнесу, проте, наскільки мені відомо, договір, що укладається між двома сторонами, одна з яких працює в українському легальному полі, повинен укладатись обома мовами одночасно із превалюванням суті тексту однією за узгодженням (як у пункті 14.2.4). Звідси запитання – чи надасте Ви двомовний варіант цього договору для підписання?_

_На заключення, хотів би підкреслити, що до цього моменту наша взаємодія не викликала нарікань, а доменне ім’я та інформація на вебсайті і так були створені мною (залученим підрядником) за згоди співробітників українського офісу Bolt власним коштом лише для однієї цілі – залучення водіїв та автопарків, поглиблення нашої плідної співпраці. Сенс такого вебсайту існує лише в парадигмі співпраці з Bolt. То чи не краще було б продовжити взаємодію без будь-який зобов’язань у частині питання прав на доменне ім’я?_

This is a matter rather for the CS product team. I know they are already reworking their automatic compensations logic, however, until then we do not have any good solutions for you.

It is not optimal for our team to check these riders user-by-user. To give some context then the fraud team rather focuses on significant financial fraud cases and patterns. Further, as this fraud happens in relation to our product allowing/freely giving them the refunds it is the automatisation itself causing the fraud. Think of it this way: asking for a refund is not fraud and our product giving refunds without any further checks is a product fault.

We are assisting and working closely with the product team, but as I said it is not optimal to escalate these cases to fraud until the product gets reworked. We can recommend you action the matter on a case-by-case basis as they are reported/discovered, similar to refund fraud that CS has a process for.

Cheers,
Francesca

From initial research we should add four security-headers: 

X-frame-options

* Either {{sameorigin}} or {{deny}}
* Do you guys know if [bolt.eu|http://bolt.eu/] is used inside an iframe or frame somewhere, where we want?

X-content-type-options

* {{nosniff}}
* I think only IE does it, but couldn't find a definitive list of browsers still trying to predict file types

Permissions-Policy (Formerly Feature-Policy)

* A lot of stuff we could disable, but maybe only the most invasive ones
* microphone, camera, payments, display-capture

Content-security-policy

* {{upgrade-insecure-requests}} or {{block-all-mixed-content}} (if upgrade is defined, then no need for block-all-mixed-content)
* {{object-src: none}} disables support for legacy elements that do not get security updates
* Ideally we would have src protection also with nonce, but this might be a bigger undertaking to make sure that all our scripts are still loading.
* Since this can be quite breaking, it is recommended to start with only reporting version
* Strict CSP defined - [https://csp.withgoogle.com/docs/strict-csp.html|https://csp.withgoogle.com/docs/strict-csp.html|smart-link]

Hey! Thanks for the long description to get a better understanding of the process. 

* Even though using Infobip removes the risks deriving from personal phone usage, there are still severe compliance and security risks related to using Whatsapp. As said previously, low security of Whatsapp exposes us to data breaches and may also result in lack of compliance whereby we are not in line with the GDPR (which foresees that when using data processors, we need to make sure they adhere to same necessary standard of security and compliance as we do). As background, Whatsapp was even fined 5.5 mln euros by the Irish data protection authority beginning of this year, so they have also been under regulatory scrutiny for their data processing practices.
* So, taking all of this into account, the privacy team recommends not using Whatsapp and to prefer internal systems. However, we understand that these risks need to be weighed with other possible risks\benefits and it will be a business decision. 
* If business will move on with using Whatsapp, then make sure to put in place a reasonable retention time (you should only process data as long as you need it, referring to these messages), we can also help to assess the proportionality of such a period. You should also make sure the data is processed securely every step of the way, especially when the documents are moved from Infobip to our systems whereby I understand data is downloaded to personal computers. You can reach out to our Info Sec team [~accountid:6061907490e3950069a3a5d3] to explore more about a secure transfer in this situation and who can advise on data handling until there is a solution (like making sure data is deleted from the personal computer asap)
* Last, but not least, we would recommend to remove the paragraph in the end of the message starting with “If you’d wish to stop receiving..” since such wording is mainly used for direct marketing messages but in this case, it is a service related message.

Rejecting the bug: the only reliable way to match a GitHub user with an admin-panel user is to search GitHub user via email. Github search API allows searching by emails only for public emails that were explicitly set as public. Public emails are visible in the profile, which might be a security concern. Better approach would be to integrate OKTA with github and use OKTA as a single source of truth for the user-related data. But it goes beyond this task and requires more effort. As this bug affects only a small amount of users and could be fixed by making a commit to the bolt-server, we decided to reject this bug.

Hi there,

Apologies for the slight delay. 

I will try my best to explain this as best as I can. Pretty much it is not a single failed payment that has caused the user’s risk to be higher. Their company and its users have been connected to other companies through profiling. These connections can happen through (e.g) payment methods, device types or in this case email domain profiling. 

So we monitor bigger groups of users based on their different types of connections which are both direct and indirect. The related group here reached a certain threshold of payment issues meaning most of the users (also read companies) had issues and this also raised the risk (score) of the entire group and single users. I cannot share the specific numbers but I can confirm this is a HIGH % of the group’s activity. 

There is no direct restriction that follows this ‘profiling’. Each user on our service has their score (which can be also described as fraud risk) and only when certain score thresholds are reached then actions follow that ensure the user is a trusted or good user and, upon successful recovery, these restrictions/actioned are lessened. If the score from one profiling would have been the only factor, the user would not have been directed to verification, however, there were rather multiple ‘risks’ that ended up raising the user's score and the automatic recovery process was offered. 

In short, it is our overall risk profiling due to the group of which the user is a part of that suggested user confirmation/verification. The user always has an opportunity to opt out of verification and continue through alternative methods. Further, upon significant good history (and hence a good added score) the risk would cancel itself out as we would have “proof” of previous trusted behaviour and, again, the user would not reach the (personal) thresholds for these actions to be proposed. And here the user did not have a such significant good history to counteract the risk. 

It seems I have lost who exactly is requesting this specific information (I guess the user?) but if you still need to proceed, would you mind specifying where this information would go exactly? I am not able to share the specifics outside of our Fraud team. My own question here is that if the user is against verification then why did they proceed with it? 😄 

Hope it helps,

# "The sum of the amounts received by the taxpayer during the calendar year”
# “The sum of the amounts paid by the person liable, during the same calendar year, to users of the linking service” 

* only consider payments we collect - *exclude cash*.
* consider the net payments we collect, which means we *reduce the “amounts received” with promocodes and Bolt borne refunds*
* Consider the net payouts, meaning we can *reduce the “amounts paid” with driver borne refunds*
* We can consider the amounts *including VAT if that’s easier to obtain*

{color:#ff5630}Example with a 12€ trip with a 20% (2,40) commission:{color}

* *Promocode*: Bolt offers a 2€ promocode. Bolt collects 10€ and pays the driver 12€ minus commission.
** 1) sum of amounts received: 10€ (12€ minus promocode of 2€)
** 2) sum of amounts paid: 9,60€ (12€ minus 2,40 commission)
* *Refund*:
** {color:#36b37e}*Bolt*{color} *bears the cost* of a full refund:
*** 1) sum of amounts received: : 0€ (12€ minus refund of 12 €)
*** 2) sum of amounts paid: 9,60€ (12€ minus 2,40 commission)
** {color:#4c9aff}*Driver*{color} *bears the cost* of a full refund:
*** 1) sum of amounts received: : 0€ (12€ minus refund of 12 €)
*** 2) sum of amounts paid: -2,40€ (12€ minus 12€ refund minus 2,40 commission)

This topic is predominantly legal issue that should be covered in service T&Cs, however there is a privacy aspect associated with this safety event.

According to clause 2.4  of the Courier Terms and Conditions, the courier is obliged to ensure the full confidentiality of the personal data received from Bolt (including address of the eater). The courier shall ensure that access to the personal data received from Bolt shall be given to only
those representatives of the courier who need require it strictly in relation to the performance of
their duties and that all such representatives are subject to a confidentiality obligation.

Having another person during the delivery can affect eater’s privacy, as eater’s address would be then exposed to third party, not associated with Bolt and not subject to confidentiality obligations. Therefore, this specific case would be deemed a violation of courier’s privacy obligations expressed in Schedule 2 to the General Terms to Bolt Food delivery service.

Hey Olivier! We need some changes indeed on both prenotice and probation periods:

For *Probation Periods*:

* Fixed term employees with up to 6 month contract duration - probation needs to be *15 days*
* Fixed term employees with more that 6 month contracts (usually a year) - probation needs to be *30 days*
* Regular employees - probation period varies from 90 to 240 days based on job level:  P5/M4 and above: 240 days; P3/M2, P4/M3: 180 days; P1, P2/M1: 90 days (_not sure if it’s possible to set it up like that?_)
** Ideally notifications for 90 days probation periods are sent 30 days before; notifications for the remaining should be sent at least 60 days before.

For *Notice Periods*:

* If seniority is over 2 years, notice period is 2 months, for *all* employees
* If seniority is less than 2 year, then:
** if employee is *fixed term* and with seniority of less than 6 months, than notice period should be 15 days
** if employee is *fixed term* and with seniority of more than 6 months and less than 2 years, than notice period should be 30 days
** if employee is *regular*, in *probation* period:
*** if seniority is more than 2 months, then prenotice period needs to be 7 days
*** if seniority is more than 4 months, then prenotice period needs to be 15 days
** if employee is *regular*, with *successful probation* period, then prenotice is 30 days



All these notice periods only apply for *voluntary* resignations - involuntary resignations depend on several legal processes and are not met with the same rules.

Furthermore, notifications regarding fixed-term contracts end should be sent to managers 30 days before contract end date, to give enough time to prepare for communications - ideally the comm for People Partner about the contract end should also be sent at the same time. 

Thanks!
